content: Preterm infants require a high intake of protein to support their growth and development. While breast milk offers numerous benefits for these infants, its protein content is highly variable and often insufficient to meet the demands of rapid growth. This review, updated in 2020, aimed to evaluate whether supplementing human milk with additional protein improves growth, body composition, cardio-metabolic health, and neurodevelopmental outcomes in preterm infants, without causing significant adverse effects. To address this question, researchers conducted a systematic search of databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) and MEDLINE via PubMed, as of August 23, 2019. They also reviewed clinical trial registries and reference lists of relevant articles to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials. Eligible studies included hospitalized preterm infants fed human milk, who were randomly assigned to receive either additional protein supplementation or no supplementation. Two independent reviewers extracted data, assessed the risk of bias, and evaluated the quality of evidence using the GRADE methodology. Meta-analyses were performed using risk ratios (RR) for categorical outcomes and mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). A fixed-effect model was used, and subgroup or sensitivity analyses were planned to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. The review included six RCTs involving a total of 204 preterm infants. The risk of bias in most studies was unclear due to insufficient reporting of methodological details. Low-quality evidence suggested that protein supplementation of human milk may increase in-hospital growth rates in terms of weight (MD 3.82 g/kg/day, 95% CI 2.94 to 4.7; five RCTs, 101 infants; I² = 73%), length (MD 0.12 cm/week, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.17; four RCTs, 68 infants; I² = 89%), and head circumference (MD 0.06 cm/week, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.12; four RCTs, 68 infants; I² = 84%). However, protein supplementation may also be associated with longer hospital stays (MD 18.5 days, 95% CI 4.39 to 32.61; one RCT, 20 infants; very low-quality evidence). The evidence regarding the impact of protein supplementation on feeding intolerance (RR 2.70, 95% CI 0.13 to 58.24; one RCT, 17 infants) and necrotizing enterocolitis (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.07 to 17.12; one RCT, 76 infants) was of very low quality, making the effects uncertain. No data were available on the influence of protein supplementation on neurodevelopmental outcomes. In conclusion, low-quality evidence indicates that protein supplementation of human milk may enhance short-term growth in preterm infants. However, the small sample sizes, low precision, and very low-quality evidence regarding hospital stay duration, feeding intolerance, and necrotizing enterocolitis limit the ability to draw firm conclusions about these outcomes. Additionally, no data were available on outcomes after hospital discharge. The findings may not be applicable to low-resource settings, as none of the included studies were conducted in such environments. Since protein supplementation is now commonly included as part of multi-nutrient fortifiers, future research should focus on comparing different protein levels in multi-component fortifiers. These studies should aim to assess the effects on hospital stay duration, safety, and long-term outcomes, including growth, body composition, cardio-metabolic health, and neurodevelopment.
